    13	  knowable-from-the-record: local-comprehension
    14	---
    15	
    16	# Implementation principles
    17	
    18	## What this set governs
    19	
    20	This is the implementation-scope principle set: the one stated
    21	definition of good implementation engineering — what counts as good
    22	when a shop, Bounded Context or lead, builds what it owns. It is a peer
    23	of the working-scope set, [Founding principles](principles.md), which
    24	governs how every activity is performed, and of the architecture-scope
    25	set, [Architecture principles](architecture-principles.md), which
    26	governs what the designed system must look like; this set governs what
    27	a built implementation must be. Backticked slugs cite principles; a
    28	slug not defined in this document is defined in one of those two sets.
    29	
    30	Two roles carry this set, each defined as a role definition under
    31	`roles/`: the maker role, which makes an implementation, and the
    32	checking role, which checks it against this set. Each role's definition
    33	names this set as the source its accountabilities are drawn from and
    34	restates none of its rules. The terms Bounded Context, shop, activity,
    35	acceptance scenario, feature, initiative, implementation, maker role,
    36	checking role, and evidence are defined in the [glossary](glossary.md).
    37	These terms carry a fixed sense in this set:
    38	
    39	- **effect** — what an acceptance scenario's Then states will be
    40	  observable; a scenario *holds* when its effect is observable.
    41	- **design** — what `bidirectional-conformance` makes authoritative:
    42	  descriptions, contracts, and recorded decisions, together with the
    43	  criteria and constraints that ride on a scenario by name in its
    44	  feature. A design element is any one of these.
    45	- **design change** — a change to what an implementation is built to:
    46	  an assigned scenario or a design element added, altered, or retired.
    47	  A design change is *recorded* when the feature or the design carries
    48	  it before the build that relies on it; a change present only in the
    49	  code is unrecorded.
    50	- **mechanism** — the tools, the order of steps, and the techniques by
    51	  which an implementation was made.
    52	- **appetite** and **cost** — the appetite is the initiative's bound on
    53	  what the product will spend, time or capacity, as the initiative's
    54	  Appetite section states it; the cost is what an implementation
    55	  consumed of it, in the same unit.
    56	
    57	Where a principle here applies a working-scope or architecture-scope
    58	principle at the implementation level, this document declares the
    59	lineage in its frontmatter — `derives-from` maps the principle in this
    60	set to the principle it applies — instead of restating the rule as a
    61	second authority.
    62	
    63	## What a good principle looks like
    64	
    65	This section restates the shared definition from the
    66	[principle-set typedef](artifacts/principle-set.md) so this document can
    67	be read alone; the restatement is a rendering, not a second authority.
    68	
    69	A principle is a standing rule, in four parts: a name, a statement, a
    70	rationale, and implications.
    71	
    72	- The **statement** is the rule. It carries the only normative keywords
    73	  (MUST, SHOULD, MAY — interpreted per BCP 14 when, and only when, they
    74	  appear in capitals) and is testable: shown a piece of work, you can
    75	  answer yes or no. A statement carrying more than one obligation
    76	  presents one obligation per bullet.
    77	- The **rationale** says why the rule earns its place: the failure it
    78	  prevents, shown as a generic example; well-known external references
    79	  may support it, the product's own history never appears. Rationales
    80	  stay prose.
    81	- The **implications** are the price tag: one implication per bullet,
    82	  the concrete change each named actor absorbs to honor the rule. They
    83	  add no obligations — every implication must be derivable from the
    84	  statement, or it is a misfiled rule.
    85	
    86	A principle is good when its statement is testable (TOGAF, The Open
    87	Group Architecture Framework: understandable, complete, consistent), it
    88	rejects work we would otherwise do (Jared Spool, "Creating Great Design
    89	Principles"), it directs without prescribing method (Richard Rumelt,
    90	*Good Strategy Bad Strategy*), it is not a claim every shop would make
    91	(Patrick Lencioni, "Make Your Values Mean Something", Harvard Business
    92	Review, 2002), and it implies at least one practice and one check. Two
    93	of those tests carry the weight at this scope: a principle here judges
    94	an implementation by the effect it produces and never names a tool, a
    95	step order, or a technique as the mark of good (Rumelt's test); and it
    96	holds as a standing rule across cases, never as the memory of one
    97	incident (the generic-failure rule every rationale obeys). The fitness
    98	screen at the end of this document applies these tests to the
    99	principles above it.
   100	
   101	---
   102	
   103	## Build what the scenarios state, and only that (`built-to-the-scenario`)
   104	
   105	**Statement.**
   106	
   107	- An implementation MUST make every acceptance scenario assigned to it
   108	  hold.
   109	- An implementation MUST NOT add behavior that no assigned scenario and
   110	  no design element calls for.
   111	- Where an assigned scenario cannot hold without behavior the design
   112	  does not call for, the maker role MUST ask for a design change that
   113	  calls for that behavior.
   114	- The maker role MUST NOT build that behavior before the design change
   115	  is recorded.
   116	- The checking role MUST fail an implementation on an assigned scenario
   117	  that does not hold, or on a change that no assigned scenario and no
   118	  design element calls for.
   119	
   120	**Rationale.** The assigned scenarios are the one statement of what the
   121	work is for that maker, checker, and consumer all read before the
   122	build. An implementation judged against anything else — the maker's
   123	sense of what was probably wanted, the neighbouring feature that looked
   124	cheap while the code was open — is judged against a target only its
   125	maker can see. The familiar failure runs both ways at once: a builder
   126	handed three scenarios delivers two of them and a configuration option
   127	nobody asked for; the consumer finds the missing scenario in use, and
   128	within a month something depends on the extra option, so it can never
   129	be removed. Beck's rule in *Extreme Programming Explained* — you aren't
   130	going to need it — names the reverse half. The two-direction check is
   131	`bidirectional-conformance`'s, which this principle applies to one
   132	implementation: forward, every assigned scenario built; reverse,
   133	nothing built that the design never called for.
   134	
   135	**Implications.**
   136	
   137	- The maker role builds from the assigned scenarios and the design
   138	  elements riding on them, and from no scenario it was not assigned.
   139	- The maker role, on finding a scenario that cannot hold without a
   140	  design change, stops and asks for the change; it does not build first
   141	  and record afterward.
   142	- The checking role checks both directions — each assigned scenario
   143	  holds, and each change traces to an assigned scenario or a design
   144	  element — and fails a change that traces to neither, whatever its
   145	  merit.
   146	
   147	## The effect is shown, not declared (`effect-shown`)
   148	
   149	**Statement.**
   150	
   151	- An implementation MUST NOT count as done until evidence exists that
   152	  each assigned scenario's effect occurred.
   153	- That evidence MUST be a record the checking role can read without the
   154	  maker role's account of it.
   155	- The maker role's own declaration that an effect occurred MUST NOT
   156	  stand as evidence.
   157	- The verdict on the evidence MUST sit with the checking role, never
   158	  with the maker role.
   159	
   160	**Rationale.** A declaration of done costs nothing to make and is wrong
   161	at the same rate whether it is honest or not, because the maker is the
   162	one reader who cannot see what they did not build. A shop that takes
   163	the maker's word has moved its check to the first consumer, at the
   164	worst moment and the highest price: the familiar failure is the build
   165	reported complete and never exercised, whose consumer finds the
   166	scenario that never held. Segregation of duties — the internal-control
   167	rule that whoever performs a transaction does not also approve it (the
   168	COSO framework) — is the same rule applied to money. This principle
   169	applies the working set's `define-good-up-front`, whose check sits with
   170	a different role, to the one activity where the maker's word is most
   171	often taken.
   172	
   173	**Implications.**
   174	
   175	- The maker role produces the evidence with the implementation; an
   176	  implementation without it is not submitted.
   177	- The checking role reads the evidence, not the maker's account of it,
   178	  and returns fail where the evidence does not exist, whatever the
   179	  maker reports.
   180	- The checking role, and no other role, marks a scenario passed.
   181	
   182	## The effect is judged; the mechanism is the maker's (`effect-not-mechanism`)
   183	
   184	**Statement.**
   185	
   186	- A check of an implementation MUST judge it by the effect it produces
   187	  against its assigned scenarios.
   188	- A check MUST NOT fail an implementation for the tool, step order, or
   189	  technique that produced it where no design element names one.
   190	- The maker role MAY choose any mechanism the design's stated
   191	  constraints admit.
   192	
   193	**Rationale.** A mechanism mandated as the mark of good is a proxy: it
   194	was once seen alongside good results, and the mandate outlives the
   195	correlation. The familiar failure is the shop that reviews for the
   196	technique's presence — passes work that performed the technique and
   197	produced nothing, fails work that produced the effect another way —
   198	until its makers learn to perform the technique rather than the effect.
   199	Goodhart's law names what happens: when a measure becomes a target, it
   200	stops being a good measure. A mandate on mechanism is also, almost
   201	always, written for one kind of maker; judging by effect is what lets
   202	`actor-neutral-discipline` hold in the build, where a human maker and
   203	an agent maker meet the same bar.
   204	
   205	**Implications.**
   206	
   207	- The checking role writes its verdict in terms of the scenarios'
   208	  effects; a verdict that cites only a mechanism has no standing.
   209	- The maker role chooses its tools and its order for itself, and owes
   210	  no defence of a mechanism the design did not constrain.
   211	- The checking role, when it fails an implementation on a mechanism,
   212	  cites the design element that names that mechanism; a mechanism
   213	  preference that no design element states binds no one.
   214	
   215	## Nothing that held stops holding (`nothing-lost`)
   216	
   217	**Statement.**
   218	
   219	- After an implementation, every scenario that held in what the shop
   220	  owns before it MUST still hold.
   221	- Where a new scenario can hold only if an earlier one stops holding,
   222	  the earlier scenario MUST be retired by a recorded design change
   223	  before the build, not lost by it.
   224	- The checking role MUST fail an implementation on a scenario that held
   225	  before it and does not hold after it.
   226	
   227	**Rationale.** An implementation does not land alone; it lands in a
   228	system where every scenario that already holds is a promise someone
   229	relies on. The familiar failure is the shop that checks each change on
   230	its own scenarios only: a year on, the scenarios that still hold are a
   231	subset of the ones ever accepted, nobody can say which subset, and
   232	every consumer re-tests what the shop already claimed. Lehman's laws of
   233	software evolution record the drift — a system's quality declines
   234	unless work is spent to hold it — and so name the price of not spending
   235	it. The retirement route is `bidirectional-conformance`'s: a design
   236	change is a recorded activity, and retirement is gated on it.
   237	
   238	**Implications.**
   239	
   240	- The maker role shows that the earlier scenarios still hold as part of
   241	  its evidence, not only that the new ones do.
   242	- The checking role fails an implementation on a lost scenario as it
   243	  would on a missing one.
   244	- Whoever needs an earlier scenario to stop holding asks for the design
   245	  change that retires it before the build; the maker role does not
   246	  retire a scenario by building over it.
   247	
   248	## What changed is readable from the record (`knowable-from-the-record`)
   249	
   250	**Statement.**
   251	
   252	- An implementation MUST leave what it changed, and the scenario or
   253	  design element each change answers to, readable from the shop's own
   254	  records.
   255	- Those records MUST suffice for the next maker role to take up the
   256	  same part without the previous maker's account.
   257	- The checking role MUST fail an implementation whose records do not
   258	  suffice, whether or not its scenarios hold.
   259	
   260	**Rationale.** The maker who built a part carries what it does and why
   261	in their head, and the next maker either asks, reads everything, or
   262	rebuilds it. The familiar failure is the part whose only description is
   263	a person — "ask whoever wrote it" — which works until that person is
   264	elsewhere. For an agent maker the failure is literal: the next maker is
   265	a fresh context with no memory of the last one, and whatever is not in
   266	the record did not happen. Parnas and Clements, "A Rational Design
   267	Process: How and Why to Fake It" (1986), make the case that the record,
   268	not the process that produced it, is what the next reader uses. This
   269	principle applies `local-comprehension` to one implementation: working
   270	inside a shop is done from that shop's own records and code, so an
   271	implementation leaves records that level can work from.
   272	
   273	**Implications.**
   274	
   275	- The maker role writes what changed and why into the shop's records
   276	  with the implementation, before submitting it for the check.
   277	- The checking role reads the record as part of the check; an
   278	  implementation the checker can follow only by asking the maker fails
   279	  on its record, whether or not its scenarios hold.
   280	- The next maker role, finding a record that does not suffice, reports
   281	  the shortfall rather than reconstructing the earlier maker's intent
   282	  from the code.
   283	
   284	## Cost lands on the initiative (`cost-on-the-initiative`)
   285	
   286	**Statement.**
   287	
   288	- An implementation MUST stay within the appetite of the initiative its
   289	  feature belongs to.
   290	- The maker role MUST stop an implementation that will not finish
   291	  within that appetite rather than overrun it.
   292	- The maker role MUST report the stop to the initiative's owner.
   293	- The cost of an implementation MUST be recorded on that initiative.
   294	- The checking role MUST NOT give a verdict on an implementation whose
   295	  cost is not recorded on its initiative.
   296	
   297	**Rationale.** The appetite is the whole content of the bet: the
   298	authority decided what the problem was worth. An implementation that
   299	spends past it on its own has changed the bet without the bettor, and
   300	one whose cost no record holds cannot be priced against its outcome
   301	afterward, so the next bet is made blind. The familiar failure is the
   302	feature "almost done" for the third week of its two, which nobody
   303	decides to stop because nobody is told. Shape Up (Singer, Basecamp)
   304	fixes the time and varies the scope, with a circuit breaker that ends
   305	the work when the time is up; this principle asks less — stop and
   306	report, and let the owner decide.
   307	
   308	**Implications.**
   309	
   310	- The maker role reads the appetite before it starts and reports, as
   311	  soon as it can see it, that the work will not fit; it does not extend
   312	  the work quietly.
   313	- The maker role, on stopping, hands the decision on scope or appetite
   314	  to the initiative's owner and does not take it itself.
   315	- The maker role records the cost, in the appetite's unit, with the
   316	  implementation.
   317	- The checking role confirms the cost is recorded on the initiative
   318	  before it gives a verdict; an implementation without a cost entry
   319	  waits on the maker role for the entry.
   320	
   321	---
   322	
   323	## Fitness screen (the intro's tests; sources: TOGAF, Spool, Rumelt, Lencioni)
   324	
   325	| Screen | built-to-the-scenario | effect-shown | effect-not-mechanism | nothing-lost | knowable-from-the-record | cost-on-the-initiative |
   326	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

   329	| Not fluff, not a goal-in-disguise (Rumelt) | pass — judges by the scenarios held; names no tool, order, or technique | pass — judges by evidence of the effect; names no form of test | pass — the rule is method-neutrality itself | pass — judges by what still holds; names no regression technique | pass — judges by what the next maker can do from the record; names no documentation format | pass — judges by the bound kept and the cost recorded; names no estimating method |

   333	| Implications derivable and actor-named, one per bullet (judged) | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass |

    11	
    12	# Base writing style
    13	
    14	Rules for everything written for a human reader. A document type's
    15	format sits on top; it never overrides these rules.
    16	
    17	## Say what, not why
    18	
    19	State the point first, then what supports it — document, section, and
    20	paragraph each open with their point. No reasoning, options, or
    21	self-argument in an artifact's body; put that in the Document History
    22	row. Do not explain what the reader can already see.
    23	
    24	## Sentences and words
    25	
    26	- Short sentences, one idea each.
    27	- Active voice, a named actor: "Reviewers delete unlinked checks," not
    28	  "Unlinked checks are subject to deletion."
    29	- Plain, common words: "use" not "utilize."
    30	- No metaphor as a technical term — say the literal thing.
    31	- Explain an insider reference in one plain sentence, or cut it.
    32	- When work is waiting, say what it is waiting on and on whom, in
    33	  plain words; never use a shorthand for the state of the work in its
    34	  place.
    35	- Never use a banned word; the lint holds the list.
    36	
    37	## History rows
    38	
    39	One sentence: what changed, under what.
    40	
    41	## Word targets
    42

    44	|---|---|
    45	| Role prompt (rendered) | 400 |
    46	| Feature | 1,000 |

    49	| Edges row (feature) | 20 |
    50	| Initiative | 400 |
    51	| Process definition | 800 |
    52	| Guidance record | 600 |
    53	| Decision record | 500 |

    58	targets.

     3	id: adr-2026-09-16-scenario-evidence-form
     4	title: Evidence of a scenario's effect is the shop's pass/fail where executable, the checking role's mark where not
     5	status: recorded
     6	version: 1
     7	date: 2026-09-16
     8	decided-by: product-authority
     9	right: guardrail
    10	owner: lead-solutions-architect
    11	created: 2026-09-16
    12	updated: 2026-09-16
    13	---
    14	
    15	# ADR: Evidence of a scenario's effect is the shop's pass/fail where executable, the checking role's mark where not
    16	
    17	## 1. Context
    18	
    19	Terms, from the existing type system: a fitness set already carries
    20	`judged` and `executable` as frontmatter fields, one true and the
    21	other false, never both — the
    22	[fitness-set typedef](../basis/artifacts/fitness-set.md) treats a
    23	criterion set an automated runner can execute and a criterion set a
    24	role must read and judge as two distinct, named kinds of check. This
    25	decision applies the same distinction to a feature's scenarios.
    26	
    27	Pre-state, read from lead-shop-held records. `delivery-verified` — the
    28	working principle requiring an implementation's effect "demonstrated
    29	in the running system" before it counted done — was removed whole from
    30	the working set on 2026-09-15
    31	([basis/principles.md](../basis/principles.md) v12, Document History),
    32	under init-delivery-verified-removal, on the product authority's own
    33	words: "There is no mechanism that would be possible to implement in
    34	the current system that would meet the principle. This will need to be
    35	brought back when the system is more mature." The removal deliberately
    36	left open what a check accepts in the principle's place; nothing
    37	replaced it.
    38	
    39	feat-implementation-good (v4), authored against that gap, carries
    40	seven scenarios stating a definition of good for implementation
    41	engineering. Scenario @hash:bbccc3a1765c requires that "the checking
    42	role requires an implementation's effect shown, not declared." At the
    43	feature's add-constraints step the lead-solutions-architect role (this
    44	role) read that scenario against the removal and found no fixed
    45	mechanism naming what evidence a check accepts or which role declares
    46	it satisfied, and recorded that as a needs-decision line rather than
    47	deciding it — feat-implementation-good's Contributors section and its
    48	Edges table row "What form of evidence a check accepts... routed to
    49	adr-authoring." The same feature's own seven scenarios are themselves
    50	an instance of the open question: they are judged reads of definition
    51	documents (this typedef, the role definitions, the fitness set), not
    52	tests any runner can execute — so the question the removal left open
    53	is live in the very feature that raised it.
    54	
    55	The product authority decided this on 2026-09-16 in conversation with
    56	the lead-pm, in two statements, in order:
    57	
    58	1. "Evidence is the shop presenting the pass/fail status of the
    59	   scenario tests."
    60	2. Asked what a pass/fail is for a scenario with no executable test —
    61	   feat-implementation-good's own seven — the authority answered:
    62	   "Scenario tests means executable tests. For non-executable tests,
    63	   the checking role can mark the scenarios as passed."
    64	
    65	Forces. The authority's 2026-09-09 position
    66	([sessions/sess-2026-09-09-c.md](../sessions/sess-2026-09-09-c.md)) —
    67	"the scenario can close when the implementer shows it as complete
    68	through passing scenarios but the PM is ultimately responsible for
    69	whether the delivered feature meets the user need" — sets a level above
    70	this one (the PM's accountability, written into the lead-pm role
    71	definition under init-implementation-process) and is not restated or
    72	contradicted here; this record settles only what a check accepts as
    73	the scenario's own evidence, not what stands above it. The same
    74	session confirmed four defects in `main`'s implementation-role
    75	prompts, one of which bears directly on this decision: "the check held
    76	inside the maker's own prompt." A decision that let a maker's own
    77	declaration stand as evidence, executable or not, would recreate that
    78	defect; the authority's second statement instead names a role other
    79	than the maker — "the checking role" — as the one who marks a
    80	non-executable scenario passed, and feat-implementation-good's own
    81	scenario 4 ("two implementation roles carry the definition, one making
    82	and one checking... neither role is both") already requires that the
    83	checking role and the maker role are not the same role. This decision
    84	does not itself name who fills the checking role; it states only what
    85	counts as evidence once a checking role exists, so it adds no route
    86	back to the defect.
    87	
    88	Options that were real.
    89	
    90	- **One evidence form for every scenario — require every scenario be
    91	  made executable before it can be checked.** Not chosen: the
    92	  authority's own second statement rules it out directly ("for
    93	  non-executable tests, the checking role can mark the scenarios as
    94	  passed") — the authority was asked exactly this question, in the
    95	  concrete case of feat-implementation-good's seven read-based
    96	  scenarios, and declined to force executability as a precondition.
    97	- **The maker's own declaration counts as evidence, for either form.**
    98	  Not chosen: this is the fourth confirmed defect verbatim ("the check
    99	  held inside the maker's own prompt"). The authority's first statement
   100	  requires the shop to present a test's pass/fail status rather than a
   101	  maker's say-so, and the second names the checking role, not the
   102	  maker, as the one who marks a non-executable scenario passed.
   103	
   104	No other option was put to the authority in the recorded conversation;
   105	these two are the ones the two statements, read together, foreclose.
   106	
   107	Self-evaluation against the [adr fitness set](../basis/fitness/adr.fitness.md),
   108	scenario by scenario: (1) the title names the decision in one line and
   109	§2 states it as one sentence a reader can act on, its two forms one
   110	conditional rule rather than two decisions — pass. (2) this Context
   111	states the pre-state and forces with their sources (the removal, the
   112	feature, the two sessions cited) and names two real options with the
   113	reason each was declined — pass. (3) §2 names `decided-by:
   114	product-authority` and `right: guardrail`, standing on the authority's
   115	own word per the typedef's rule — pass. (4) each Consequences bullet
   116	names what changes, for whom, and its cost, and the two bounds on
   117	Bounded Context shops are stated as bounds — pass. (5) §4 states the
   118	decision is hard to reverse once built against, and names its
   119	triggers — pass. (6) §2.1 states the principles screen result,
   120	conformance, against every principle in the set — pass. No fail found
   121	against this fitness set.
   122	
   123	## 2. Decision
   124	
   125	Where a feature's scenario has an executable test, the evidence a
   126	check accepts that the scenario's effect occurred is the shop
   127	presenting that test's pass/fail status; where a scenario has no
   128	executable test, the evidence is the checking role — a role other than
   129	the scenario's maker — marking the scenario passed.
   130	
   131	### 2.1 Principles screen
   132	
   133	Screened against the
   134	[architecture principle set](../basis/architecture-principles.md):
   135	conforms, no exception carried.
   136	
   137	- `actor-neutral-discipline` — the rule attaches to the scenario (does
   138	  it carry an executable test or not), never to which kind of actor
   139	  built or checks it; a human checking role and an agent checking role
   140	  mark a non-executable scenario passed under the identical rule, and
   141	  neither gets a lighter bar for being a particular kind of actor.
   142	- `bidirectional-conformance` — this decision states what forward
   143	  conformance evidence a check accepts (did the built scenario do what
   144	  the design said) for the implementation activity generally; it does
   145	  not touch the reverse direction or gate any retirement, so it neither
   146	  conforms further ground it does not need nor conflicts.
   147	- `contracts-between-contexts` — no Bounded Context contract is in
   148	  scope; the decision governs how any shop's own check reads its own
   149	  scenarios, not a channel between two Bounded Contexts.
   150	- `knowable-shape` — no first-class entity (Bounded Context or shop) is
   151	  created or described here; nothing in this decision touches that
   152	  principle's obligation.
   153	- `local-comprehension` — the decision does not change what artifacts
   154	  any level must read; it names what a check accepts as evidence within
   155	  work already scoped to its level.
   156	- `intent-provenance` — the decision does not route intent; it does not
   157	  bear on this principle.
   158	
   159	## 3. Consequences
   160	
   161	- **A shop with an executable scenario test presents that test's
   162	  pass/fail status as its evidence.** What changes: the check no longer
   163	  accepts a maker's declaration that the scenario is done — it requires
   164	  the test's own pass/fail output. For whom: every shop that implements,
   165	  Bounded Context or lead, whose maker role must run and present the
   166	  test; the checking role, who reads the presented status rather than
   167	  taking the maker's word. Cost: an executable scenario cannot close
   168	  without a runnable test existing and being run. Bound on Bounded
   169	  Context shops: a BC shop performing implementation MUST present the
   170	  pass/fail status of a scenario's executable test as that scenario's
   171	  evidence; it MUST NOT substitute its own declaration.
   172	- **A shop with a non-executable scenario has the checking role mark it
   173	  passed.** What changes: where no runner can execute the scenario (a
   174	  judged read of definition documents, as feat-implementation-good's own
   175	  seven scenarios are), the checking role's mark is the evidence, in
   176	  place of a test result that cannot exist. For whom: the checking
   177	  role, who takes on a judgment accountability for these scenarios that
   178	  it did not carry under the removed principle; the maker role, which
   179	  gains no path to mark its own scenario passed. Cost: a non-executable
   180	  scenario's evidence rests on the checking role's judgment rather than
   181	  a reproducible test run, which is weaker evidence than the executable
   182	  form and cannot be independently re-executed later. Bound on Bounded
   183	  Context shops: a BC shop performing implementation MUST route a
   184	  non-executable scenario's pass/fail to a checking role distinct from
   185	  the scenario's maker; it MUST NOT mark its own non-executable
   186	  scenario passed.
   187	- **The maker/checking role split, already required by
   188	  feat-implementation-good's scenario 4 and the working set's
   189	  `define-good-up-front`, is load-bearing for both forms.** What
   190	  changes: nothing new is required of that split by this decision, but
   191	  both evidence forms depend on it — the executable form because the
   192	  checking role, not the maker, is the one reading the presented status
   193	  at check time, and the non-executable form because the mark comes
   194	  from the checking role by name. Cost: none beyond what
   195	  feat-implementation-good already commits to. Forecloses: a
   196	  non-executable scenario closing on the maker's own mark under either
   197	  form.
   198	
   199	Two questions this decision does not settle — the subject named them
   200	neither directly nor by omission the architect can resolve from the
   201	pre-state — are put to the lead-pm role as asks, each with the default
   202	this record acts on for this pass, per the `asks: [lead-pm]` provision
   203	of the `author` step:
   204	
   205	- **Ask 1** (kind: `scope`) — Presented to whom, and where the evidence
   206	  lands. The authority said the shop "presents" the pass/fail status,
   207	  and named no destination. `reconcile-and-close` (the router role's
   208	  process for consuming a BC's completed dispatch) is the obvious
   209	  existing landing point, but feat-implementation-good's own scope note
   210	  says the lead shop's implementation scenarios sit in the lead shop's
   211	  own tree with no dispatch, so `reconcile-and-close` as written may not
   212	  reach them. Default, acted on here: the evidence lands wherever the
   213	  work item that carries the scenario closes — `reconcile-and-close` for
   214	  a dispatched BC scenario, and the equivalent close step of the
   215	  implementation process (not yet defined; session two of
   216	  init-implementation-process) for the lead shop's own. No process
   217	  definition is amended by this record to carry that default; it binds
   218	  only this record's reading until stated in the processes themselves.
   219	- **Ask 2** (kind: `reserved-decision`) — Whether the shop's presented
   220	  pass/fail stands on its own or must be independently re-run by the
   221	  lead. The authority's first statement says the shop "presents" the
   222	  status; it does not say whether presentation alone suffices. Default,
   223	  acted on here: it stands on its own — the authority's word is
   224	  "presenting," not "re-running," and requiring an independent re-run
   225	  is a stronger bar the authority was not asked about and did not
   226	  state; this default may prove wrong and is the lead-pm's to correct.
   227	
   228	## 4. Reversibility
   229	
   230	Hard to reverse once the implementation process (init-implementation-process,
   231	session two) and the maker/checking role definitions are built against
   232	it: both role definitions and the process's check step will be written
   233	to this evidence bar, and every scenario closed under it will have been
   234	closed on this reading of "evidence." Reversing later means rewriting
   235	both role definitions, the process's check step, and re-judging
   236	whatever closed under the old bar. Review triggers: the authority's own
   237	stated intent to bring `delivery-verified` back "when the system is
   238	more mature" — that reinstatement, once it happens, replaces or
   239	subsumes this record's non-executable-scenario form with whatever
   240	mechanism the mature system supports; or either ask above resolving
   241	against its default.
   242	
   243	## Document History
   244	
   245	| Version | Date | Kind | Entry |
   246	|---|---|---|---|
   247	| 1 | 2026-09-16 | update | Authored by the lead-solutions-architect role from the needs-decision line this role wrote at feature-authoring's add-constraints step on feat-implementation-good (v4), anchor lead-ft3ad, per the product authority's decision of 2026-09-16 taken in conversation with the lead-pm (two statements, quoted in Context). Pre-state read from lead-shop-held records alone: feat-implementation-good, basis/principles.md v12's Document History, sessions/sess-2026-09-15-a.md, sessions/sess-2026-09-09-c.md, the fitness-set typedef's judged/executable fields, and basis/architecture-principles.md. One decision, stated with its two forms as the subject requires. Two questions the subject leaves open put to lead-pm as asks, each with a default acted on for this pass, per the process's first-pass rule. |
   248	| 1 | 2026-09-16 | state | draft → recorded, by the `record` step. Evaluation against the [adr fitness set](../basis/fitness/adr.fitness.md): all six scenarios pass, per the scenario-by-scenario self-evaluation stated in §1 Context — one decision named and stated actionably; the context carrying forces, sources, and two real options each with the reason declined; the decider and right named and standing on the authority's own word; every consequence priced for whom and at what cost, with both Bounded-Context bounds stated as bounds; reversibility stated with its triggers; the principles screen stated. Evaluation against the [architecture principle set](../basis/architecture-principles.md): conformance on all six principles, per §2.1 — `actor-neutral-discipline` (the rule attaches to the scenario, not the actor kind checking or making it), `bidirectional-conformance` (states forward-evidence acceptance only, touches neither the reverse direction nor a retirement gate), `contracts-between-contexts`, `knowable-shape`, `local-comprehension`, and `intent-provenance` (each screened and found not implicated or not conflicting, per §2.1); no exception carried, nothing absorbed as a deviation. Made by the lead-solutions-architect role. |

   151	  created or described here; nothing in this decision touches that
   152	  principle's obligation.

   154	  any level must read; it names what a check accepts as evidence within
   155	  work already scoped to its level.
   156	- `intent-provenance` — the decision does not route intent; it does not
   157	  bear on this principle.
   158	
   159	## 3. Consequences
   160	
   161	- **A shop with an executable scenario test presents that test's
   162	  pass/fail status as its evidence.** What changes: the check no longer
   163	  accepts a maker's declaration that the scenario is done — it requires
   164	  the test's own pass/fail output. For whom: every shop that implements,
   165	  Bounded Context or lead, whose maker role must run and present the
   166	  test; the checking role, who reads the presented status rather than
   167	  taking the maker's word. Cost: an executable scenario cannot close
   168	  without a runnable test existing and being run. Bound on Bounded
   169	  Context shops: a BC shop performing implementation MUST present the
   170	  pass/fail status of a scenario's executable test as that scenario's
   171	  evidence; it MUST NOT substitute its own declaration.
   172	- **A shop with a non-executable scenario has the checking role mark it
   173	  passed.** What changes: where no runner can execute the scenario (a
   174	  judged read of definition documents, as feat-implementation-good's own
   175	  seven scenarios are), the checking role's mark is the evidence, in
   176	  place of a test result that cannot exist. For whom: the checking
   177	  role, who takes on a judgment accountability for these scenarios that
   178	  it did not carry under the removed principle; the maker role, which
   179	  gains no path to mark its own scenario passed. Cost: a non-executable
   180	  scenario's evidence rests on the checking role's judgment rather than
   181	  a reproducible test run, which is weaker evidence than the executable
   182	  form and cannot be independently re-executed later. Bound on Bounded
   183	  Context shops: a BC shop performing implementation MUST route a
   184	  non-executable scenario's pass/fail to a checking role distinct from
   185	  the scenario's maker; it MUST NOT mark its own non-executable
   186	  scenario passed.

   188	  feat-implementation-good's scenario 4 and the working set's
   189	  `define-good-up-front`, is load-bearing for both forms.** What
   190	  changes: nothing new is required of that split by this decision, but
   191	  both evidence forms depend on it — the executable form because the
   192	  checking role, not the maker, is the one reading the presented status
   193	  at check time, and the non-executable form because the mark comes
   194	  from the checking role by name. Cost: none beyond what
   195	  feat-implementation-good already commits to. Forecloses: a
   196	  non-executable scenario closing on the maker's own mark under either
   197	  form.

   206	  lands. The authority said the shop "presents" the pass/fail status,
   207	  and named no destination. `reconcile-and-close` (the router role's
   208	  process for consuming a BC's completed dispatch) is the obvious
   209	  existing landing point, but feat-implementation-good's own scope note
   210	  says the lead shop's implementation scenarios sit in the lead shop's
   211	  own tree with no dispatch, so `reconcile-and-close` as written may not
   212	  reach them. Default, acted on here: the evidence lands wherever the
   213	  work item that carries the scenario closes — `reconcile-and-close` for

# compile-process (produced from the answer of `basis/tools/compile_process.py`)

Compiles a process definition: checks that every `$ref` in its data block has a source that defines the type, regenerates the Mermaid flow diagram in the definition's `## Flow (compiled)` section, and — on request — renders the definition's loadable skill, whose only prose is the step prompts, verbatim, each agent-run step closing with the line naming its declared outputs as the form its return takes and with the banned-words line read from the lint. Use it after a process definition changes, and to place or refresh the definition's skill at the agent's load point.

Uses: [compile](#compile), [compile-skill](#compile-skill).

## compile

Checks the definition's `$ref` sources and `result`, regenerates the flow diagram, and writes it back into the definition's `## Flow (compiled)` section in place — the one write; nothing else in the definition changes and no skill is written.

Invocation:

```sh
python3 basis/tools/compile_process.py <definition>
```

Takes:
- `<definition>` — the path of the process definition, for example basis/processes/skill-rendering.md; its `$ref` sources resolve relative to that path (required)

Returns (text): one line on standard output, `<definition>: flow diagram regenerated (<n> steps)`; exit status 0; the diagram written into the definition

Fails:

| code | exit status | condition | next step |
|---|---|---|---|
| `unreadable` | 2 | no file exists at <definition>, or it cannot be read; one line on standard error beginning `unreadable:` names the path; nothing is written | give the path of an existing process definition and run the invocation again |
| `unparseable` | 1 | the definition has no front-matter, its front-matter or a yaml block does not parse, or no yaml block carries `steps` and `start`; one line on standard error beginning `unparseable:` names the path and the defect; nothing is written | repair the definition at the named defect and run the invocation again |
| `check-failed` | 1 | the definition does not compile: a `$ref` without a `from:` source, a source that does not exist or does not define the type, a `result` that is not a declared data value, no `## Flow (compiled)` section to fill, or a step the renderer cannot render; one line on standard error beginning `check-failed:` names the path and the defect; nothing is written | repair the definition at the named defect (the process-definition typedef states the rules) and run the invocation again |
| `unwritable` | 1 | the definition, or the skill at <out>, could not be written; one line on standard error beginning `unwritable:` names the path and the reason | make the path writable, or give one that is, and run the invocation again |
| `usage` | 2 | the arguments are not one of the two invocations this tool states — no definition, more than one, `--skill` without a path, or an unknown option; one line on standard error beginning `usage:` names them; nothing is written | run the invocation the use states, as written |

## compile-skill

Does what `compile` does, then renders the definition's skill — front-matter with `generated: true`, `source`, and `source-digest` over the definition's text, its `ask-cap` and `hold-after` where the definition carries them, the purpose, guiding statement, diagram, and every step with its prompt verbatim, each agent-run step's prompt closing with its outputs line and the banned-words line — and writes it to <out>, creating the directories, overwriting what stands there, a hand edit included.

Invocation:

```sh
python3 basis/tools/compile_process.py <definition> --skill <out>
```

Takes:

# Basis index

The `basis/` tree is the shop's definition corpus. Every activity on
the `rebaseline` branch operates through these definitions; nothing
here is advisory.

## What lives where

- [`principles.md`](principles.md) — the working-scope principle set:
  how every activity is performed.
- [`architecture-principles.md`](architecture-principles.md) — the
  architecture-scope principle set: how the system is designed.
- [`glossary.md`](glossary.md) — the defined-term list, combined with
  every schema element name.
- `artifacts/` — artifact typedefs, rooted at
  [`artifacts/definition.md`](artifacts/definition.md), which carries
  the requirements every definition document inherits (frontmatter
  identity, version, Document History).
- `types/` — data types passed between process steps.
- `processes/` — process definitions; every activity belongs to one.
- `guidelines/` — prose quality rules per artifact type, layered on
  [`guidelines/base-writing-style.md`](guidelines/base-writing-style.md).
- `fitness/` — judged Given/When/Then scenario sets per artifact type.
- For a type whose typedef carries Writing rules and Fitness scenarios
  sections (the [artifact-typedef typedef](artifacts/artifact-typedef.md)
  §Required sections 6–7), its guideline and fitness set at those two
  paths are renderings of the typedef — marked `generated: true`,
  naming their `source` and its `source-digest` — produced by
  [`tools/compile_typedef.py`](tools/compile_typedef.py) and kept
  current by the typedef-rendering process
  (`processes/typedef-rendering.md`, pending); never edited by hand.
- `roles/` — role definitions (roles, accountabilities, competencies).
- `guidance/` at the repository root — implementation guidance
  records, one per Bounded Context per assignment, written by the
  [scenario-assignment process](processes/scenario-assignment.md)'s
  assign step; the directory may not exist yet. The type's typedef is
  [`artifacts/implementation-guidance.md`](artifacts/implementation-guidance.md),
  and its two produced texts are the guideline
  [`guidelines/implementation-guidance.md`](guidelines/implementation-guidance.md)
  and the fitness set
  [`fitness/implementation-guidance.fitness.md`](fitness/implementation-guidance.fitness.md).
- generated skill renderings live at the agent's load point —
  `.claude/skills/` at the repository root — maintained by the
  [skill-rendering process](processes/skill-rendering.md); never edited
  by hand. Three source kinds stand there: a process skill, rendered
  from an approved process definition by `compile_process.py`; a tool
  skill, produced by [`tools/compile_tool.py`](tools/compile_tool.py)
  from a framework tool's answer to the standard question — the tool
  run with `--describe`, its answer an instance of the

For each scenario, decide which Bounded Context owns the behavior it states — from the decomposition and that context's contract at contracts, never from the scenario's wording alone — and write a single @bounded-context: tag on it. A scenario whose behavior no context owns, that two contexts would each have to own, or whose owning context differs from the shop Contributors names as its owner, goes to unowned with the reason; do not guess. Then, for each context tagged, read its pre-state — the state of the design: its contract at contracts and the feature repository at repository — and sweep the repository for conflicts: a scenario that contradicts one already specified there goes to unowned with the conflict as its reason. Write one assignment entry per context with the @hash: values of its scenarios and the pre-state read. When no scenario is unowned, write for each context tagged one implementation guidance record at guidance/-.md — the feature's id and the context's name as tagged — by its guideline: what its scenarios change at the level you may see (its contract, the guardrails that apply, where the cross-context flow touches it; for the lead shop's own definitions, the definitions and tools to change), the references to the contract and the scenario hashes, and what not to do; evaluate it against its fitness set before you write it; it is a historical record of this assignment and is not sent. Put each record's path in guidance. Return the tagged feature. next: route - id: route name: Route on ownership run-by: {execution: runtime} inputs: [unowned] branches: - label: "success exit: every scenario owned" when: size(unowned) == 0 next: dispatch - else: return - id: return name: Return the feature with the unowned scenarios named run-by: {role: lead-solutions-architect, execution: agent} inputs: [feature, unowned] outputs: [feature] prompt: | Write a review entry into the feature's Document History naming each unowned scenario and its reason and set the feature's status to "returned" — the returned feature is the handoff to the PO role, which reads its status. # Artifact type: definition

## Identity and ancestry

- **Type:** `definition` — the generic root for documents that state what
  good looks like for something else: a process, a document type, a role,
  a term list, a rule set. Specializations (e.g. `process-definition`,
  `artifact-typedef`) declare it in their ancestry, so a validator that
  knows only `definition` can check any definition document against the
  two requirements below.
- **Produced by:** seed drafting, or governed evolution of an approved
  definition. **Consumed by:** every agent whose work the definition
  governs; compilers and validators that render or check against it.

## Required frontmatter

`type`, `id`, `status` (draft | approved | superseded), `owner` (the role
that approves changes), `version` (integer, starting at 1; bumped on
every content update), `created`, `updated`; `approved` (date of the most recent approval) once approved — retained
through a later draft amendment to mark the last approved version.

## Required sections

1. An **opening** that states what the document defines before the
   first section heading.
2. A closing **checks section** (its heading contains "check") — every
   definition implies at least one check; a definition no check can cite
   does not govern anything.
3. A **Document History** section, the last section of the document: a
   table `| Version | Date | Kind | Entry |` where Kind is `update` (a
   content change; bumps the version), `review` (a review round and its
   verdict; cites the version reviewed), or `state` (a status change,
   e.g. draft → approved; cites the version it applies to). All
   change-log, review-log, and state-log content lives here — inline
   amendment notes and formal review-log frontmatter structures (e.g. a
   `verified-by` block) are ruled out. Generated renderings are exempt:
   their history is their source's.

## Commitment (Definition of Done)

A definition is done when the governed work can be performed and checked
from it alone. **Consequence on failure:** the definition — and any
activity that would depend on it — does not enter the system
(`define-good-up-front`).

## Sources

Deming's operational definitions (a definition others can work from:
test, criterion, decision); the `define-good-up-front` principle.

## Derived review checklist

- Frontmatter complete; owner named; version present. *(schema)*
- The opening states what the document defines. *(§Required sections 1)*
- At least one derived check exists and cites a clause. *(§Required sections 2)*
- Document History is the last section; no inline amendment notes or
  review-log frontmatter remain — mechanical. *(§Required sections 3)*

# Process: Implementation

**Purpose:** Take one assignment's scenarios to a checked
implementation: the maker role builds every scenario assigned, the
checking role evaluates the build against
[Implementation principles](../implementation-principles.md), and a
failed check repairs under a round cap until it passes or the cap is
reached. One process for every shop that implements; every step here
runs by a fixed role or the runtime alone, so a lead-shop execution
needs no dispatch and no mailbox call.

**Guiding statement:** Implementation principles is the whole of what
good looks like for the build: the maker builds to it and the checking
role judges by it alone, never by the maker's account of the work and
never by a mechanism no design element names.

**Outcomes:**
- O1. A shop looking for how to execute an implementation finds this
  one process, not an approach chosen anew per build — witnessed by
  this definition's frontmatter, the one `use-when` for building or
  repairing an assignment, and by its carried skill, rendered at the
  agent's load point by `compile_process.py`; no second definition
  covers the same job.
- O2. The maker role produces the implementation and the checking role
  evaluates it before an execution counts done — witnessed by `make`'s
  and `check`'s `run-by`, two fixed, different role ids, and by
  `route-check`: the only path to `record`'s pass verdict runs through
  `check`, and `check` runs only after `make`.
- O3. The lead shop executes this process on what it owns with no step
  requiring dispatch to a Bounded Context shop or mailbox work —
  witnessed by the step list: every step runs by a fixed role, agent
  or runtime, and none names `shop-msg`, a Bounded Context shop, or a
  mailbox call.
- O4. A completed execution's cost lands on the initiative whose
  feature the executed scenario belongs to — witnessed by this
  definition naming no cost step: an execution's bead already records
  the initiative it serves
  ([feat-initiative-cost-rollup](../../features/feat-initiative-cost-rollup.md),
  delivered) and its cost rows write at session close
  ([feat-run-measurement](../../features/feat-run-measurement.md),
  delivered), both independent of this definition.

**Roles:** the maker —
[`../roles/implementation-maker.md`](../roles/implementation-maker.md)
(builds the assignment's scenarios and leaves what changed, and why,
in each changed artifact's own record; fixed in `make`'s and
`record`'s `run-by`). The checking role —
[`../roles/implementation-checker.md`](../roles/implementation-checker.md)
(gives the pass/fail verdict from evidence read, never from the
maker's account; fixed in `check`'s `run-by`, and held to no write
tool, so it never records its own verdict). Fixing both `make`'s and
`check`'s `run-by` to literal role ids, on small-change.md's
precedent, is what makes "the checker is never the maker" a mechanical
fact of this definition rather than a value a caller could set to the
same role. A change whose checking role must be another role is a
change to this definition, filed as the gap it is, never a run-time
substitution.

**Carried by:** `.claude/skills/implementation/SKILL.md` — generated
from this definition by
[`../tools/compile_process.py`](../tools/compile_process.py), never
edited by hand.

## Flow (compiled)

```mermaid

```

## Data

`feature` is the path of the feature the assignment's scenarios belong
to (typedef: [`../artifacts/feature.md`](../artifacts/feature.md));
`guidance` is the path of the implementation guidance record for this
assignment (typedef:
[`../artifacts/implementation-guidance.md`](../artifacts/implementation-guidance.md)),
whose frontmatter names the `@hash:` values assigned and whose body is
written to be actionable alone — `make` and `check` read guidance and
feature and nothing else, per its own commitment. Neither carries a
Decomposition or a request: this process has no route, no bet, and no
check of record — every scenario it takes up already passed
feature-authoring and scenario-assignment, and the appetite and cost
disciplines the maker role owes are its own accountabilities under
[Implementation principles](../implementation-principles.md), not
restated here as steps.

`changed` is the paths `make` changed, returned each round and read by
`check`, which fails a path in `changed` that traces to no scenario
`guidance` assigns and no design element. `check_verdict` and
`check_finding` are the checking role's verdict and, on a fail, the
statement or rule that fails, quoted — the evidence form
[adr-2026-09-16-scenario-evidence-form](../../decisions/adr-2026-09-16-scenario-evidence-form.md)
fixes: an assigned scenario's presented pass/fail status where one is
executable, the checking role's own mark where none is. `round` counts
make-then-check cycles; `round_cap` bounds them. This definition
declares no cost value: an execution's cost is carried by its bead and
its session's cost rows, delivered by feat-run-measurement and
feat-initiative-cost-rollup and unchanged by this process, per the
finding that no new cost mechanism is needed
(guidance/feat-implementation-process-shopsystem-product.md, item 4).

```yaml
data:
  feature: {type: string, format: uri-reference}
  guidance: {type: string, format: uri-reference}
  changed: {type: array, items: {type: string}, initial: []}
  check_verdict: {type: string, enum: [pass, fail]}
  check_finding: {type: string, initial: ""}
  round: {type: integer, initial: 1}
  round_cap: {type: integer, initial: 3}
```

## Steps

```yaml
start: make
parameters: [feature, guidance]
steps:
  - id: make
    name: Build the assigned scenarios
    run-by: {role: implementation-maker, execution: agent}
    inputs: [guidance, feature, check_finding, round]
    outputs: [changed]
    prompt: |
      Read guidance and, by the @hash: values it assigns, the
      feature's scenarios — nothing else; guidance is written to be
      actionable with the assigned scenarios alone. Build every
      assigned scenario so it holds, through each changed artifact's
      own producing rules: amended under its own type's rules, a
      rendering re-rendered by its own tool and never edited by hand,
      its Document History gaining one update row citing guidance by
      path and this round, its version bumped. Add no behavior that no
      assigned scenario and no design element calls for. Where a
      scenario cannot hold without a design change guidance does not
      cover, stop and report that rather than building it unrecorded.
      When check_finding is not empty this is a repair round: repair
      what it quotes, and show that every scenario that held before
      this round still holds. Evaluate what you built against
      Implementation principles yourself before you return, and add
      that evaluation to the same update row. Return changed, the
      paths you touched this round.
    next: check

  - id: check
    name: Check the build against Implementation principles
    run-by: {role: implementation-checker, execution: agent}
    inputs: [guidance, feature, changed]
    outputs: [check_verdict, check_finding]
    prompt: |
      Read guidance, the feature's assigned scenarios, and the
      artifacts at changed — nothing else. You are not the maker: your
      verdict is judged against Implementation principles alone, never
      against the maker's account. For each assigned scenario, per
      adr-2026-09-16-scenario-evidence-form: where it carries an
      executable test, read the shop's presented pass/fail status as
      its evidence; where it does not, mark it yourself from what you
      read. Verdict fail on a scenario that does not hold, on a change
      in changed that traces to no assigned scenario and no design
      element, on a scenario that held before this round and does not
      hold after it, or on a changed artifact whose record does not
      suffice for the next maker. Verdict pass only when every
      assigned scenario holds and every change conforms; otherwise
      fail, with check_finding the statement or rule that fails,
      quoted, and what fails it. Return the verdict and the finding —
      empty on pass.
    next: route-check

  - id: route-check
    name: Route on the check
    run-by: {execution: runtime}
    inputs: [check_verdict, round, round_cap]
    branches:
      - label: "success exit: every assigned scenario holds — record the verdict"
        when: check_verdict == "pass"
        next: record
      - label: "failsafe exit: round >= round_cap — record the verdict as failed at the cap"
        when: round >= round_cap
        next: record
      - else: advance-round

  - id: advance-round
    name: Advance the round
    run-by: {execution: runtime}
    inputs: [round]
    set:
      round: round + 1
    next: make

  - id: record
    name: Record the checking role's verdict
    run-by: {role: implementation-maker, execution: agent}
    inputs: [changed, check_verdict, check_finding, round, round_cap]
    outputs: [changed]
    prompt: |
      For each path in changed, write one review-kind Document History
      row citing the version reviewed, the checking role, the round,
      and the verdict as check_verdict and check_finding give it,
      transcribed as given — you do not rejudge it. Where check_verdict
      is fail and round is at round_cap, the row also states the
      scenario stands unresolved at the cap. Return changed.
    next: end
```

| O4 | no data value or step here names a cost field; the bead-initiative and session-close mechanisms are cited in Data as the delivered features that carry it | mechanical | Data |

## Steps

```yaml
start: make
parameters: [feature, guidance]
steps:
  - id: make
    name: Build the assigned scenarios
    run-by: {role: implementation-maker, execution: agent}
    inputs: [guidance, feature, check_finding, round]
    outputs: [changed]
    prompt: |
      Read guidance and, by the @hash: values it assigns, the
      feature's scenarios — nothing else; guidance is written to be
      actionable with the assigned scenarios alone. Build every
      assigned scenario so it holds, through each changed artifact's
      own producing rules: amended under its own type's rules, a
      rendering re-rendered by its own tool and never edited by hand,
      its Document History gaining one update row citing guidance by
      path and this round, its version bumped. Add no behavior that no
      assigned scenario and no design element calls for. Where a
      scenario cannot hold without a design change guidance does not
      cover, stop and report that rather than building it unrecorded.
      When check_finding is not empty this is a repair round: repair
      what it quotes, and show that every scenario that held before
      this round still holds. Evaluate what you built against
      Implementation principles yourself before you return, and add
      that evaluation to the same update row. Return changed, the
      paths you touched this round.
    next: check

  - id: check
    name: Check the build against Implementation principles
    run-by: {role: implementation-checker, execution: agent}
    inputs: [guidance, feature, changed]
    outputs: [check_verdict, check_finding]
    prompt: |
      Read guidance, the feature's assigned scenarios, and the
      artifacts at changed — nothing else. You are not the maker: your
      verdict is judged against Implementation principles alone, never
      against the maker's account. For each assigned scenario, per
      adr-2026-09-16-scenario-evidence-form: where it carries an
      executable test, read the shop's presented pass/fail status as
      its evidence; where it does not, mark it yourself from what you
      read. Verdict fail on a scenario that does not hold, on a change
      in changed that traces to no assigned scenario and no design
      element, on a scenario that held before this round and does not
      hold after it, or on a changed artifact whose record does not
      suffice for the next maker. Verdict pass only when every
      assigned scenario holds and every change conforms; otherwise
      fail, with check_finding the statement or rule that fails,
      quoted, and what fails it. Return the verdict and the finding —
      empty on pass.
    next: route-check

  - id: route-check
    name: Route on the check
    run-by: {execution: runtime}
    inputs: [check_verdict, round, round_cap]
    branches:
      - label: "success exit: every assigned scenario holds — record the verdict"
        when: check_verdict == "pass"
        next: record
      - label: "failsafe exit: round >= round_cap — record the verdict as failed at the cap"
        when: round >= round_cap
        next: record
      - else: advance-round

  - id: advance-round
    name: Advance the round
    run-by: {execution: runtime}
    inputs: [round]
    set:
      round: round + 1
    next: make

  - id: record
    name: Record the checking role's verdict
    run-by: {role: implementation-maker, execution: agent}
    inputs: [changed, check_verdict, check_finding, round, round_cap]
    outputs: [changed]
    prompt: |
      For each path in changed, write one review-kind Document History
      row citing the version reviewed, the checking role, the round,
      and the verdict as check_verdict and check_finding give it,
      transcribed as given — you do not rejudge it. Where check_verdict
      is fail and round is at round_cap, the row also states the
      scenario stands unresolved at the cap. Return changed.
    next: end
```

## What was built

- **`/home/vscode/rebaseline/basis/processes/implementation.md`** — the new process-definition (`implementation-process`, `status: draft`, v1). Steps: `make` (agent, role `implementation-maker`) → `check` (agent, role `implementation-checker`) → `route-check` (runtime branch) → `record` (agent, role `implementation-maker`, transcribes the checking role's verdict, since that role holds no write tool) → `end`, with a `round`/`round_cap`-bounded repair loop (`advance-round` → back to `make`).
- **`/home/vscode/rebaseline/.claude/skills/implementation/SKILL.md`** — rendered by `compile_process.py`, `generated: true`, digest matching the source.

## The four scenarios, what makes each hold

Per `adr-2026-09-16-scenario-evidence-form`, none of these has an executable test (each is a judged read of a definition document), so I state what a reader checks directly.

- **`@hash:e996f2d086ab`** (one defined process, not chosen anew) — `basis/processes/implementation.md` is the one process-definition for this job; its frontmatter `annotations.claude-code.use-when` states the one triggering condition, distinct from `small-change.md`'s; it is rendered at the agent's load point (`.claude/skills/implementation/SKILL.md`). A reader confirms no other file under `basis/processes/` claims the same `use-when`, and that the skill's digest matches the source.
- **`@hash:afe74d3e9ff5`** (maker then checker before done) — `make.run-by` names `implementation-maker`, `check.run-by` names `implementation-checker` (lines 157, 182 of the definition) — two fixed, distinct role ids. Every path to `record` (the step preceding `end`) is gated by `route-check` on `check_verdict`, `check`'s own output; no branch reaches `record` without `check` having run. `check`'s prompt states "You are not the maker" and judges only by Implementation principles and the ADR's evidence form.
- **`@hash:f90002450ad9`** (no dispatch, lead shop executes itself) — every step's `run-by` is one of `{role: implementation-maker|implementation-checker, execution: agent}` or `{execution: runtime}`; `grep -n "shop-msg"` over the file returns nothing, and no step is `execution: sub-process` to a Bounded Context shop.
- **`@hash:0e92f2731640`** (cost lands on the initiative) — holds through infrastructure this process deliberately adds nothing to: `feat-initiative-cost-rollup` (`status: delivered`, scenario `@hash:5d23e3458539`: an execution's bead records the initiative it serves) and `feat-run-measurement` (`status: delivered`: a session close writes a cost row per agent step). The Data section states this explicitly and declares no cost field; the Document History cites guidance item 4 as the finding this rests on.

## Fitness evaluation (process-definition fitness set, recorded in the file's Document History)

Scenario 1 (renderings correspond): pass, confirmed after compiling — diagram and skill both `generated: true`, matching the Steps section. Scenario 2 (outcomes witnessed): pass, each of O1–O4 names a checkable step/branch/frontmatter element. Scenario 3 (loop exits declared): pass, the one cycle carries a labeled success exit and a labeled round-cap exit. Scenario 4 (declared reads only): pass, each step's prompt references only its declared inputs. Scenario 5 (artifact result): pass by omission, on `skill-rendering.md`'s precedent — no `result` declared since the execution's value is a set of changed definitions, pinned by the outcomes. Scenario 6 (prose placement): pass, prose only in `prompt` fields and body text.

`python3 basis/tools/lint_basis.py --process basis/processes/implementation.md` → `PASS: 0 violation(s)`. Full `python3 basis/tools/lint_basis.py` → last line `PASS: 0 violation(s)` (preceded by `vocabulary residue: 19 files` — a pre-existing, report-only count across the corpus; my file introduced no new residue, and I reworded a "run-time" phrase that would have added one).

## Decisions I made on my own authority (flagging for review)

- **The verdict-recording design**: since `implementation-checker` has no write tool, `record` is run by `implementation-maker`, which transcribes the checker's already-decided verdict onto each changed artifact's own Document History as a `review`-kind row (the `definition` typedef's own Kind enum) — it does not re-judge. This is a design choice, not stated verbatim in the guidance.
- **No appetite/stop branch or ask mechanism**: `cost-on-the-initiative`'s stop-and-report duty is left as the maker role's own accountability (already stated in `implementation-maker.md`), not re-encoded as a process branch — on the typedef's own rule that "role files carry identity, never sequencing."
- **No `basis/README.md` change**: its `processes/` entry is generic (no per-file listing), so nothing there needed updating; checked, not skipped.
- **Did not commit or push.** The primer states session close requires a successful `git push`, but committing wasn't part of this task's explicit instructions and the git-safety protocol says only commit when asked — `basis/processes/implementation.md` and `.claude/skills/implementation/` are untracked and ready for the orchestrating session to commit.
- Since the process I built doesn't exist yet to run itself on its own construction, the four scenario checks above are my own read as the finishing role of the declared bootstrap exception, not an independent `implementation-checker` execution — consistent with the Appetite's framing that this build (and `feat-implementation-good`'s) are the last made outside the process being defined.
